chataignier.resume: A nourishing fruit, rich in starch. Its look-alike, the horse chestnut, is poisonous.
identification: Husk bristling with fine, long, very dense spines (like a hedgehog)
2 to 3 nuts per husk, flattened on one side, with a small hairy tip
Simple, long leaves (15–25 cm), edged with pointed teeth

sosies.diff: Husk with a few short, widely spaced spikes, a single round, smooth nut without a tip, fan-shaped leaves with 5–7 leaflets.

usages: Roasted on the embers (score the shell first so it doesn't burst) or boiled 20–30 min.
Raw, it is astringent and hard to digest.

hetre.resume: Beech dominates many European forests. Its small triangular seeds can be eaten in moderation.
identification: Smooth grey bark, straight trunk
Oval leaves with a wavy edge, slightly hairy at the margin
Four-valved husk containing 2 shiny three-sided seeds
usages: Shell then roast: cooking reduces fagin, an irritant in large amounts.
Eat in small amounts (a handful).

noisetier.resume: Hazelnuts can still be found on the ground in early November, often already emptied by animals.
identification: Multi-stemmed shrub, shiny light-brown bark
Rounded, double-toothed leaves, rough to the touch
Nut in a fringed green husk
usages: Raw or roasted. A hazelnut with a small hole is empty (larva or rodent).
Preferably gather from the ground away from paths (animal droppings).

eglantier.resume: The fruit of the wild rose. Best after the first frosts, when it softens.
identification: Thorny shrub with arching stems, hooked prickles
Oval, smooth, orange-red fruit, 1.5–2 cm, with the remains of the calyx at the tip
Compound leaves of 5 to 7 toothed leaflets

sosies.nom: Poisonous red berries (yew, bittersweet, holly, honeysuckle)
sosies.diff: None has the oval shape of the rose hip with the dried calyx at the tip, nor the prickly stems. If in doubt, don't eat.

usages: Open the fruit and remove the seeds and inner hairs: they irritate the mouth and digestive tract.
The pulp can be eaten raw when fully ripe, or as a tea (strain the hairs out carefully).

prunellier.resume: Small, very sour blue-black plums, softened by frost. Don't crunch the stones.
identification: Very thorny shrub (long, hard spines on the twigs)
Round blue-black fruits, 1 cm, covered with a waxy bloom
Grows in hedges and forest edges

sosies.diff: Shiny black berries in clusters, without a bluish bloom, on a shrub without thorns.

usages: Pick after a frost (or put them in the freezer): the astringency decreases.
Don't crunch or swallow the stones in quantity (cyanogenic compounds).

aubepine.resume: Small, mealy red berries, very common at forest edges.
identification: Thorny shrub, leaves deeply cut into 3 to 7 lobes
Oval red berries, 1 cm, in clusters, a single hard stone

sosies.diff: Check the hawthorn's lobed leaves and thorns. No lobed leaves = no hawthorn.

usages: Pulp raw or cooked, mealy, slightly sweet taste.
Spit out the stone.

sorbier.resume: Clusters of bright orange berries. Raw, they irritate the stomach: always cook them.
identification: Small tree, compound leaves of 11 to 15 toothed leaflets
Wide clusters of small orange-red berries (about 1 cm)
usages: Cook (boil) before eating: cooking destroys the irritant parasorbic acid.
Bitter taste: best as a compote or mixed with other fruit.

gland.resume: High in calories and plentiful, but full of tannins: inedible without long preparation.
identification: Leaves with rounded lobes
Smooth brown nut in a scaly cup
usages: Shell, crush, then soak, changing the water several times (or boil, renewing the water) until the bitterness has gone.
A long survival technique: rarely useful on a short bivouac.

ortie.resume: Very nutritious. The stinging hairs disappear with cooking.
identification: Square stem covered with stinging hairs
Opposite leaves, elongated heart-shaped, edged with large teeth

sosies.diff: Looks like nettle but doesn't sting. Also edible.

usages: Pick the top leaves with gloves or by pinching firmly.
In soup or blanched 1–2 min.

pissenlit.resume: Rosette of toothed leaves: leaves and roots are edible.
identification: Rosette at ground level, deeply toothed leaves
White latex when you break the leaf or the flower stalk
A single yellow flower per hollow stalk
usages: Young leaves in salad (bitter in winter), roasted root.
Wash anything growing at ground level thoroughly (see Fox).

oenanthe.resume: One of the most poisonous plants in Europe. Grows by water: beware along rivers and ditches.
identification: Large umbellifer of banks and wet ditches
Roots in fleshy spindles, sap that turns yellow in the air
White flowers in umbels

sosies.diff: Simple rule: never eat a wild umbellifer (umbrella-shaped flowers) unless you're an expert. Several are deadly.

usages: Avoid touching it with bare hands if possible, eat nothing.

if.resume: A conifer with cup-shaped red berries. Seed and foliage are highly poisonous.
identification: Flat, dark green needles, without a resinous smell
Open, cup-shaped red “berry” with a dark seed in the centre
usages: Eat nothing. Don't use its wood to skewer food.

digitale.resume: Common in forest clearings on acid soil. The whole plant is poisonous to the heart.
identification: In winter: rosette of large, oval, soft and downy leaves, marked veins
In summer: spike of purple bell-shaped flowers

sosies.diff: The rosettes look alike: don't eat any downy rosette not identified with certainty.

usages: Eat nothing.

douceamere.resume: A climber of damp hedges and banks with shiny red berries, attractive and poisonous.
identification: Climbing stem, often by water
Oval, bright red, shiny berries in hanging clusters
usages: Eat nothing.

phalloide.resume: Responsible for most fatal poisonings. Symptoms come late, when the liver is already affected.
identification: Olive-green to yellowish cap, sometimes white, smooth
White gills, ring on the stem
White sac-like volva at the base (often buried: clear around the stem)

sosies.diff: NEVER eat a mushroom identified from a photo or an app. Have it checked by a mycologist or a mycological society.

usages: Eat nothing. Wash your hands after handling.

tuemouches.resume: The red mushroom with white spots from fairy tales. Common under birch and spruce.
identification: Bright red to orange cap, covered with white flakes (which rain can wash off)
White gills and stem, ring, bulbous base

sosies.diff: Yellow gills and stem. Don't try to tell them apart yourself.

usages: Eat nothing.

galere.saison: All year round, especially in autumn
galere.resume: A small brown mushroom on dead wood, containing the same toxins as the death cap.
identification: Small brown to tawny caps, in clusters on stumps
Small, fragile ring on the stem

sosies.diff: A classic and deadly confusion, even for experienced foragers.

usages: Eat nothing.

cepe.resume: The famous bolete. Edible, but only checking by an expert makes it safe to eat.
identification: Brown cap, like a bread bun
Sponge underside (tubes), white then yellow-green, doesn't turn blue
Swollen stem with a fine raised white net at the top

sosies.diff: Tubes turning pink, dark net on the stem, very bitter taste.
Red or orange pores, flesh turning blue: discard.

usages: Have every harvest checked by a mycologist before eating.

sanglier.saison: All year round · hunting in autumn
sanglier.resume: Very present in European forests. Avoids humans, except a sow with piglets or a wounded animal.
identification: Tracks: two-toed hooves with 2 dewclaws marked behind
Rooted-up ground, muddy wallows, rubbed trees
usages: Don't leave food accessible at night (hang it or keep it in the closed tent).
In autumn, driven hunts are frequent: respect the “Hunting in progress” signs and the paths.

cerf.resume: The rut has just ended. Watch at dawn and dusk at forest edges.
identification: Tracks: split hoof in an elongated heart shape, 6–9 cm
Rubbing marks on young trees, bark stripped
usages: Keep your distance, never feed them.

renard.resume: Can transmit a serious parasite (echinococcosis) through its droppings on low vegetation.
identification: Tracks: 4 toes, oval and narrow print, in a straight line
Twisted droppings, often placed prominently on a stone
usages: Cook or wash thoroughly anything picked at ground level (berries, leaves, mushrooms).

tique.resume: Less active in November, but a mild spell is enough. Check yourself after every trip.
identification: Small brown-black mite, in tall grass and bracken
usages: Trousers tucked into socks, light-coloured clothing.
Remove with a tick remover, twisting, disinfect, note the date. See a doctor if a redness spreads.
